slides.title: Motion Editing
slides.speech: So Go-with-the-Flow makes new videos. But what about the video you already have? Here's a clip on top: a bichon and a corgi racing down a sidewalk, finishing about side by side. The dots and lines are point tracks. Pink follows the bichon's face through time, red follows the corgi's. I want the corgi to win. So I drag the corgi's red track forward, and the bottom row is the output. In the red box, the corgi's out in front. Same dogs, same street. The motion is what changed. That's MotionV2V: editing the motion of a video that already exists.

slides.title: Why not GWTF?

elements.text: Anything not in frame 1 gets made up

slides.speech: So why can't Go-with-the-Flow do this? General point and flow motion control, ATI, ReVideo, and my own GWTF, is image-to-video. It only takes this first frame and generates the rest. Anything that's not in frame one, like a car that drives in at second three, gets made up, so it's not your video anymore. And the classic editing trick, invert the video back to noise and regenerate it, only works when the output lines up with the input frame by frame. Change the motion, and that breaks.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals
slides.speech: So we train a model, and the problem is data. You'd want pairs of videos with the exact same content and different motion, and those don't exist. So we make them. Start with a real video, this guy walking down the street. Cut a clip out of it. That real clip is the target, the thing the model has to output. The target is always real footage, so the model always learns to output real-looking video.

slides.title: Motion Counterfactuals
slides.speech: Then we make a fake version of that clip with different motion. That's a motion counterfactual. Either a video diffusion model fills in between two real frames, with a prompt like make him twirl, or we speed up, slow down or reverse the real frames. Then we crop and zoom to fake a camera move, that's this one. To match points, we run one tracker over the real video with the fake frames spliced in, and start points only on frames both clips share, so each dot is the same physical point in both. Training is the fake video, its tracks and the real tracks in, and the real video out.

slides.title: The Model

elements.text: Frozen CogVideoX + trained copy of 18 blocks

slides.speech: At test time: a guy roasting a marshmallow, a sleeping dog. I click points, a tracker follows them, and those are the source tracks. I drag them to where I want them to go. Those are the target tracks, in the red box. Yellow means feed the dog, pink means the dog wakes up. The model actually gets each track as a colored blob on black, one color per point. It's a frozen CogVideoX, plus a trained copy of its first eighteen blocks that reads your video and both track videos. Unlike a normal ControlNet, none of that lines up with the output, and it works because those blocks attend across all the frames.

slides.title: Results
slides.speech: First try on this basketball, the ball went through the hoop, but a second ball showed up where the original went. The other points matched the input exactly, so it copied. Two pixels of noise on the points fixed it, but that's a shortcut the model learned. Numbers: in a four-way pick, 41 people on 20 edits we made, ours won about 70%. ATI got 25, even on a stronger base model. The error columns are reconstruction on 100 real videos where we reverse half, so there's ground truth, picked so key content isn't in frame one. Reversal's in our training data, so that tests keeping content, not editing in general. Limits: past about twenty points it stops following them, chained edits drift, and we train on fake inputs but test on real ones. This is CVPR 2026, and the code's not out yet. And motion's just one kind of edit. Next, I want any edit.
